\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Bohr model}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: angular quantum number from the elliptical orbit of the Sommerfeld model | steps: ratio of semi minor to semi major axis b/a = k/n; allowed values of k; count orbits}]

If minimum and maximum distance of electron from nucleus is $r_1$ \& $r_2$ then find distance of electron from nucleus when it is at a position where line joining electron \& nucleus is perpendicular to major axis :-
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$r_1+r_2$}
\opt{B}{$r_2-r_1$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac{r_1r_2}{r_1+r_2}$}
\opt{D}{$\dfrac{2r_1r_2}{r_1+r_2}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S2-Q06, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=6, type=multi, subtopic={Bohr model}, answer={A,B,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: Bohr model with a modified force or particle | steps: quantisation and force law give radius and energy; compare with hydrogen; check statements}]
According to Bohr model, point like electrons orbit point like nucleus at particular, fixed radii. In a particular such atom with a nucleus of charge $Q=1.6\times10^{-18}$ C initially one electron is in orbital 1 at radial distance $r_1=47.7$ \AA\ from nucleus. The orbital 2 is at a radial distance $r_2=84.8$\AA. The electric force on electron in orbital 1 is $F_1$ and that in orbital 2 is $F_2$. The KE of electron in orbital 1 is $K_1$ and in orbital 2 is $K_2$.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The ratio of $\dfrac{F_1}{F_2}$ is greater than 3}
\opt{B}{$9K_1=16K_2$}
\opt{C}{When electron does a transition from orbital 1 to 2 it absorbs energy equal to 0.66 eV}
\opt{D}{$K_1-K_2=0.66$ eV}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI02-P1-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Score-I - Test 02 (31 Dec 2021)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Radioactivity}, answer={A,B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: activity, leaking radioactive isotope with time dependent rate | steps: dN/dt = R(t) - lambda N; solve linear ODE; activity lambda N; time of maximum; check | I: source term and decay both act}]
A radioactive isotope with decay constant $\lambda$, starts leaking from a nuclear reactor at $t=0$ with rate $R(t)$, where $R(t)=R_0\,(1-e^{-Kt})$. Initially there were no atoms present outside the reactor (at $t=0$).
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The number of radioactive atoms present outside the reactor at any time $t$ is $n(t)=R_0\left[\dfrac1\lambda\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\lambda-K}\left(e^{-\lambda t}-e^{-Kt}\right)\right]$.}
\opt{B}{The number of radioactive atoms present outside the reactor after a long time is $n(t)=\dfrac{R_0}{\lambda}$.}
\opt{C}{The number of radioactive atoms present outside the reactor at any time $t$ is $n(t)=R_0\left[\dfrac{1}{\lambda-K}\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)+\dfrac{1}{\lambda-K}\left(e^{-\lambda t}-e^{-Kt}\right)\right]$.}
\opt{D}{The number of radioactive atoms present outside the reactor after a long time is $n(t)=\dfrac{R_0}{\lambda-K}$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SI08-P1-PHY-S3-G5-6, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, questions={5-6}]
One important application of radioactivity is the determination of the age of archaeological or geological samples. If an object contains radioactive nuclei when it is formed, then the decay of these nuclei marks the passage of time like a clock, half of the nuclei disintegrating during each half-life. If the half-life is known, a measurement of the number of nuclei present today relative to the number present initially can give the age of the sample. The radiocarbon technique utilizes the $^{14}_{\ 6}$C isotope of carbon, which undergoes $\beta^-$ decay with a half-life of $2\times10^{11}$ sec. This isotope is present in the earth's atmosphere at an equilibrium concentration of about one atom for every $7\times10^{11}$ atoms of normal carbon $^{12}_{\ 6}$C. It is often assumed that this value has remained constant over the years because $^{14}_{\ 6}$C is created when cosmic rays interact with the earth's upper atmosphere, a production method that offsets the loss via $\beta^-$ decay. Moreover, nearly all living organisms ingest the equilibrium concentration of $^{14}_{\ 6}$C. However, once an organism dies, metabolism no longer sustains the input of $^{14}_{\ 6}$C, and $\beta$ decay causes half of the $^{14}_{\ 6}$C nuclei to disintegrate every $2\times10^{11}$ sec. Take $\ln 2=0.7$
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI09-P2-PHY-S1-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, paper=2, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={Nuclear physics}, answer={A,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: fission at rest: speeds, kinetic energies of fragments | steps: momentum conservation; energy release delta c^2; speed ratio inversely mass; kinetic energies; check statements}]
A heavy nucleus $N$, at rest, undergoes fission $N\to P+Q$, where $P$ and $Q$ are two lighter nuclei. Let $\delta=M_N-M_P-M_Q$, where $M_P$, $M_Q$ and $M_N$ are the masses of $P$, $Q$ and $N$, respectively. $E_P$ and $E_Q$ are the kinetic energies of $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The speed of $P$ and $Q$ are $v_P$ and $v_Q$, respectively. If $c$ is the speed of light, which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$E_P+E_Q=c^2\delta$}
\opt{B}{$E_P=\left(\dfrac{M_P}{M_P+M_Q}\right)c^2\delta$}

\opt{D}{The magnitude of momentum for $P$ as well as $Q$ is $c\sqrt{2\mu\delta}$, where $\mu=\dfrac{M_PM_Q}{(M_P+M_Q)}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SII33-P2-PHY-S2-G7-8, source={Score-II - Test 33 (01 Apr 2024)}, questions={7-8}]
In a gas where rms thermal speed is $v_t\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{3kT}{m}}\right)$, coulomb force will ensure that two nuclei each with charge q, cannot approach each other any closer than the distance of closest approach $r_m$. The value of $r_m$ is the distance at which their kinetic energy is completely converted to potential energy. Separation between two hydrogen nuclei in core of the sun cannot be small enough to allow fusion to occur. Known temperature that exists in the sun's core, coulomb force will cause the nuclei to remain at distance from each other equal to 100-1000 (or more) of nuclear radii $\left(\simeq10^{-15}\text{m}\right)$. So according to classical physics proton fusion reaction should not occur in sun. But if we consider quantum nature of nuclei, quantum-mechanical tunneling allows the protons to go under the coulomb barrier with a good probability. Bridging criteria for fusion was found to be $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv_t}\leqslant r_m$ where $\lambda$ is the de Broglie wavelength of moving proton when it is at large distance from the other proton. Wherever this equation is satisfied, two nuclei can approach each other arbitrarily closely so that nuclear force can lead to fusion. We find that the rms thermal speed in core of star must exceed a critical value for fusion to occur.
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SII33-P2-PHY-S2-G11-12, source={Score-II - Test 33 (01 Apr 2024)}, questions={11-12}]
In a hydrogen atom, the electron revolves around the nucleus (proton) in circular path. In addition, then electron also spins about it's own axis. Due to this spin, electron has a magnetic dipole moment $(\vec\mu)$ in direction opposite to it's spin angular momentum $\left(\vec S\right)$. As seen from the frame of electron, the electron itself is only spinning, but the proton is moving around it in a circular path with the same speed and radius as electron in ground frame. This motion of proton around electron produces a magnetic field $\left(\vec B\right)$. This magnetic field and magnetic dipole moment of electron have a mutual potential energy. If orbital angular momentum $\left(\vec L\right)$ of electron and it's spin angular momentum $\left(\vec S\right)$ are parallel, the potential energy is different from the case when they are anti parallel.
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankq}[id=SA41-P1-PHY-S3-Q09, source={Score Advanced - Test 41}, paper=1, qno=9, type=single, subtopic={Photoelectric effect}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: photoemission, an isolated zinc bead charged to negative potential | steps: photoelectron kinetic energy hc/lambda - hc/lambda0; bead at potential -V0 gives extra energy e V0 to the leaving electron; ejection continues until the bead becomes positively charged and reaches a stopping potential; maximum potential V = (hc/e)(1/lambda - 1/lambda0); charge = 4 pi eps0 r V | I: isolated bead charges up until the potential equals the stopping potential}]

(R) & Potential of the bead after prolonged irradiation is & (3) & $\dfrac{4\pi\varepsilon_0\mathrm r}{\mathrm e}\Bigl\{\dfrac{\mathrm{hc}}{\mathrm e}\Bigl(\dfrac1\lambda-\dfrac1{\lambda_0}\Bigr)+\mathrm V_0\Bigr\}$ \\ \hline
(S) & Total number of photoelectrons emitted from the bead is & (4) & $\sqrt{\dfrac{2\mathrm{hc}}{\mathrm m}\left(\dfrac1\lambda-\dfrac1{\lambda_0}\right)}$ \\ \hline
 & & (5) & None of these \\ \hline

The potential energy of a particle of mass m is given by V (x) = $\begin{cases}\mathrm E_0&0\leqslant \mathrm x\leqslant 1\\0&\mathrm x>1\end{cases}$ $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ are the de-Broglie wavelengths of the particle, when 0 $\leq$ x $\leq$ 1 and x $>$ 1 respectively. If the total energy of particle is 2E$_0$, find $(\lambda_1/\lambda_2)^2$.
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=PS06-P1-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Pre-Score (2023-24) - Test 06 (20 Nov 2023)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=single, subtopic={de Broglie waves}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, working={Printed key.}, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: relativistic energy momentum relation applied to a particle or photon | steps: use E squared = (m0 c squared) squared + (p c) squared; relation between kinetic energy and momentum; apply to the stated situation; compare options | I: choose between relativistic and classical expressions | C: algebra with the energy momentum relation}]
The energy--momentum relation is the relativistic equation relating total energy (which is also called relativistic energy) to invariant mass (which is also called rest mass) and momentum. It is the extension of mass--energy equivalence for bodies or systems with nonzero momentum. It can be written as the following equation $E=\sqrt{(m_0c^2)^2+(pc)^2}=mc^2$. This equation holds for a body or system, such as one or more particles, with total energy $E$, invariant mass $m_0$, and momentum of magnitude $p$; the constant $c$ is the speed of light. X-ray photons are scattered through an angle of $90^\circ$ by electrons initially at rest. What is the change in the wavelength of the photons? (Take rest mass of electron as $m_0$)
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$\dfrac{h}{\sqrt2\,m_0c}$}
\opt{B}{$\dfrac{\sqrt2\,h}{m_0c}$}
\opt{C}{$\dfrac{h}{m_0c}$}
\opt{D}{None}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\opt{D}{None}
\end{qoptions}

\begin{bankq}[id=JA07-P1-PHY-S2-Q10, source={JEE Advanced (2021 Series) - Test 07 (25 Apr 2021)}, paper=1, qno=10, type=multi, subtopic={Photoelectric effect}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: momentum and energy of photons in Compton scattering | steps: photon momentum h/lambda and energy hf; momentum and energy conservation with a recoiling electron; scattered photon loses energy so frequency decreases and wavelength increases; check the statements about direction and wavelength change}]
Further support for the photon model of electromagnetic waves comes from \textit{Compton scattering,} in which x-rays scatter from electrons, changing direction and frequency in the process. Classical electromagnetic wave theory cannot explain the change in frequency of the x rays on scattering, but the photon model can. Suppose an x-ray photon is moving to the right. It has a collision with a slow-moving electron, as in figure. The photon transfers energy and momentum to the electron, which recoils at a high speed. The x-ray photon loses energy, and the photon energy formula $E=hf$ tells us that its frequency must decrease. The collision looks very much like the collision between two particles.
\bfig{174.7}{JA07_p1_phy_s2_q10_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{When the x-ray photon scatters from the electron, it's speed stays the same.}
\opt{B}{When the x-ray photon scatters from the electron, it's speed decreases.}
\opt{C}{When the electron is struck by the x-ray photon, it's de Broglie wavelength decreases.}
\opt{D}{When the electron is struck by the x-ray photon, it's de Broglie wavelength stays the same.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

Moseley's law for $K_\alpha$ photon is given by $\sqrt\upsilon=a(Z-b)$ where $a$ is a universal constant and $b$ is a screening constant. Moseley's logic helps us assume $b=1$ for $K_\alpha$ photon. If there is a percentage error $=10^{-2}$ in the measurement of '$b$' due to actual orbital configuration of an atom, then the relative error in the measurement of $\upsilon$ if $Z=51$ is $p\times10^{-q}$. \opt{A}{Value of $p$ is $=4$}
\opt{B}{Value of $p$ is $=3$}
\opt{C}{Value of $q$ is $=7$}
\opt{D}{Value of $q$ is $=6$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
